But they are not immune: if you drop down to raw SQL fragments, use string interpolation in a query builder, or pass user input into a method that expects trusted SQL (like an order-by string or a raw where clause), you can reintroduce injection. So the safe practice is to keep using the ORM's parameterized interfaces and treat any raw SQL escape hatch with the same care as hand-written queries.

question: What does sargable mean, and why does it determine whether an index gets used?
directAnswer: Sargable, from Search ARGument ABLE, means a predicate is written so the engine can use an index to seek directly to the matching rows. A predicate becomes non-sargable when you wrap the indexed column in a function or expression, like WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 or WHERE UPPER(name) = ''ANA'', because the index is built on the raw column, not on the function result, so the engine must compute the function for every row and scan. Keeping the column bare on one side of the comparison preserves sargability and lets the index work.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Sargability describes whether a WHERE or JOIN predicate can be satisfied by an index seek. A sargable predicate compares the indexed column directly to a value or range; a non-sargable one transforms the column so the index no longer matches.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An index stores raw column values in sorted order. The engine can only navigate that order if the predicate is expressed against those raw values. The concept names this requirement so engineers can write index-friendly queries on purpose.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When the indexed column appears alone on one side and a constant or parameter on the other (column = value, column > value, column BETWEEN a AND b, column LIKE ''prefix%''), the engine can seek to the right place in the index. When the column is inside a function or arithmetic (function(column) = value, column + 1 = value, leading-wildcard LIKE ''%foo''), the stored order no longer corresponds to the compared values, so the engine must evaluate the expression row by row, forcing a scan. The fix is to rewrite the predicate to leave the column untouched, for example WHERE created_at >= ''2024-01-01'' AND created_at < ''2025-01-01'' instead of YEAR(created_at) = 2024.

whyImportant: Non-sargable predicates are one of the most common reasons a perfectly good index is ignored, producing slow scans that look mysterious. Recognizing and rewriting them is a high-value, frequently tested skill that turns slow queries fast without adding any new index.
realWorldExample: A query WHERE LOWER(email) = ''user@example.com'' scanned a 50-million-row table despite an index on email. Either making the column collation case-insensitive or storing a normalized lowercase column with its own index restored an index seek, dropping the query from seconds to milliseconds.

nestedTopics.title: Functions on the column kill seeks
nestedTopics.explanation: Any function or arithmetic applied to the indexed column makes the predicate non-sargable, because the index is ordered by the raw value, not the transformed one. Moving the transformation to the constant side instead (comparing the bare column to a precomputed value) keeps the predicate sargable.

nestedTopics.title: Leading wildcards in LIKE
nestedTopics.explanation: LIKE ''abc%'' is sargable because it is effectively a range on the index, but LIKE ''%abc'' is not, since matching a suffix cannot use a prefix-ordered B-tree. Suffix or substring search needs a different structure such as a trigram index or full-text index.

nestedTopics.title: Expression and functional indexes as a fix
nestedTopics.explanation: If you genuinely must filter on an expression, many databases let you create an index on that expression (a functional or computed-column index), for example an index on LOWER(email). Then the transformed predicate becomes sargable against that purpose-built index, giving you both the transformation and the seek.

followUps.question: How do you make a date-range filter sargable?
followUps.answer: Instead of applying a function to the column, like WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 or WHERE DATE(created_at) = ''2024-05-01'', I rewrite it as a half-open range on the bare column: WHERE created_at >= ''2024-01-01'' AND created_at < ''2025-01-01'' for the year, or >= the day and < the next day for a single date. The column stays untouched, so the B-tree on created_at can seek the range directly, and the half-open form correctly handles timestamps with time components.

followUps.question: Is an implicit type conversion a sargability problem?
followUps.answer: Yes, and it is a sneaky one. If an indexed column is a string but you compare it to a number, or compare a column of one collation or type to a parameter of another, the engine may implicitly convert the column, which is effectively wrapping it in a function and breaks the seek. The fix is to make the parameter's type and collation match the column exactly so no conversion is applied to the column side. This often explains a query that ignores its index for no obvious reason.

followUps.question: When is a non-sargable query actually fine?
followUps.answer: When the table is small, when the query genuinely needs most of the rows anyway, or when the predicate is on a column you would not index regardless. In those cases a scan is the right plan and forcing sargability buys nothing. Sargability matters specifically for selective predicates on large tables where an index seek would avoid reading most of the data, so I focus my rewriting effort there rather than on every query.

question: What query rewriting techniques can dramatically improve performance?
directAnswer: Query rewriting means restructuring a logically equivalent query so the optimizer can execute it more cheaply. Common high-impact rewrites include turning correlated subqueries into joins or window functions, replacing OR conditions that block index use with UNION of indexable parts, converting NOT IN to NOT EXISTS to handle NULLs and let it short-circuit, filtering early to reduce rows before joins and aggregations, and avoiding SELECT * so the engine can use covering indexes. The same result, expressed differently, can run orders of magnitude faster.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Query rewriting is the practice of changing a query's form, not its meaning, to give the optimizer a better starting point or to remove constructs that defeat indexes and efficient operators.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Optimizers are good but not omniscient; some logically equivalent forms expose better plans than others, and some constructs (correlated subqueries, OR across columns, NOT IN with NULLs) are notoriously hard for optimizers to handle well. Rewriting helps the optimizer help you.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You identify the construct causing a poor plan from the execution plan, then express the same logic in a form the optimizer handles better. For instance, a correlated subquery that re-runs per row can become a single join or a window function evaluated once. An OR across two columns that prevents index use can become a UNION of two sargable queries, each using its own index. Pushing selective filters down before joins shrinks intermediate results, the biggest lever in multi-join queries.

whyImportant: Rewriting often beats adding indexes because it costs nothing in storage or write overhead and fixes the root cause. It demonstrates deep understanding of how the optimizer thinks, which is exactly the senior-level signal interviewers look for.
realWorldExample: A report used a correlated subquery to fetch each customer's latest order date, re-running it per customer over millions of rows and taking minutes. Rewriting it as a window function (MAX(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)) computed in a single pass dropped the runtime to seconds.

nestedTopics.title: Correlated subquery to join or window
nestedTopics.explanation: A correlated subquery executes once per outer row, which is quadratic in the worst case. Rewriting it as a join (computing the needed aggregate once and joining) or as a window function (evaluating it in a single ordered pass) replaces repeated work with one set-based operation, usually a massive speedup.

nestedTopics.title: OR rewritten as UNION
nestedTopics.explanation: A predicate like WHERE a = 1 OR b = 2 often cannot use indexes on a and b together, forcing a scan. Splitting it into SELECT ... WHERE a = 1 UNION SELECT ... WHERE b = 2 lets each branch use its own index, and the engine merges the smaller results, which is often far cheaper for selective conditions.

nestedTopics.title: Filter early, aggregate late
nestedTopics.explanation: Applying selective WHERE filters before joins and aggregations shrinks the row counts that the expensive operators must process. Pushing predicates down into subqueries or CTEs, rather than filtering after a big join, reduces intermediate result sizes, which is the single biggest lever in complex multi-join queries.

followUps.question: Why can a CTE sometimes hurt performance?
followUps.answer: In some databases a CTE is an optimization fence: the engine materializes it as a temporary result and does not push outer filters into it or merge it with the surrounding query, so a filter you expected to apply early runs late on the full materialized set. PostgreSQL behaved this way before version 12 and still does for CTEs marked MATERIALIZED. The fix is to rely on the engine's inlining where available, or rewrite the CTE as a subquery or derived table so predicates can be pushed down. So CTEs aid readability but you should verify the plan on large data.

followUps.question: How does avoiding SELECT * help performance?
followUps.answer: Selecting only the columns you need lets the optimizer use a covering index that contains exactly those columns, turning a seek-plus-lookup into a single index-only scan, and it reduces the bytes read and transferred. SELECT * forces the engine to fetch every column from the base row, defeating covering indexes and pulling large columns you may not use. Beyond performance, explicit column lists also make queries robust to schema changes. So naming columns is both faster and safer.

followUps.question: What is predicate pushdown and why does it matter?
followUps.answer: Predicate pushdown is the optimizer moving filter conditions as close to the data source as possible, so rows are eliminated before expensive joins, aggregations, or transfers happen. It matters most in layered queries and distributed systems: pushing a filter into a subquery, a view, or down to a remote shard or storage layer means far less data flows upward. Writing queries so filters can be pushed down (and not blocking it with optimization fences) is one of the most effective ways to keep large queries fast.

question: How do you query and maintain very large tables (hundreds of millions to billions of rows)?
directAnswer: The core principle is to never touch more data than necessary. For queries, that means selective indexes, partition pruning, and covering indexes so you read tiny slices, plus keyset (seek) pagination instead of large OFFSETs. For maintenance, you avoid single giant transactions: you batch updates and deletes into chunks, build indexes concurrently, and use partition swaps for bulk loads and retention. The mindset shifts from running one big statement to running many small, controlled operations that do not lock the table or blow up the transaction log.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Working with very large tables is the set of techniques for keeping reads fast and writes and maintenance safe when a table is too big to scan or modify wholesale. It spans query design, indexing, partitioning, and operational procedures.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Operations that are trivial on small tables (a full scan, a single DELETE, building an index inline) become slow, lock-heavy, and risky at scale, potentially causing downtime. These techniques exist to perform the same logical work without those side effects.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On the read side, you ensure every hot query has a supporting index and, where possible, a covering one, and you use partition pruning to skip most of the data. You replace OFFSET pagination, which scans and discards skipped rows, with keyset pagination that seeks by the last-seen key. On the write and maintenance side, you split large modifications into bounded batches (say 10,000 rows per transaction) so locks and log usage stay small, build indexes with CONCURRENTLY or ONLINE options to avoid blocking, and use partition attach/detach to load or drop data instantly.

whyImportant: Most companies eventually hit a table that is too big for naive operations, and the engineer who knows how to query and maintain it without downtime is invaluable. This question separates those who have only worked at small scale from those who have operated real systems.
realWorldExample: A required UPDATE on a 1-billion-row table to backfill a column would have run for hours in one transaction, locking the table and bloating the log. Instead it was batched: update 50,000 rows at a time by primary-key range, committing each batch, with a short pause between batches. The backfill completed safely overnight with no user-visible impact.

nestedTopics.title: Keyset (seek) pagination
nestedTopics.explanation: OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 20 forces the engine to read and discard a million rows, getting slower as you page deeper. Keyset pagination instead filters WHERE id > last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20, which seeks directly via the index and stays fast at any depth. It is the standard for paging through large datasets.

nestedTopics.title: Batched modifications
nestedTopics.explanation: A single huge UPDATE or DELETE holds locks and generates a massive transaction log entry, risking timeouts and bloat. Breaking it into bounded batches, each its own transaction over a key range, keeps locks short and the log manageable, and lets the job be paused or resumed. This is the safe way to backfill or purge at scale.

nestedTopics.title: Online and concurrent index builds
nestedTopics.explanation: Building an index inline can lock the table for the duration. PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and SQL Server's ONLINE option build the index while reads and writes continue, at the cost of taking longer and needing extra care on failure. This lets you add indexes to hot tables without downtime.

followUps.question: Why is OFFSET pagination a problem at scale, and what is the alternative?
followUps.answer: OFFSET makes the database generate and then throw away all the skipped rows before returning the page, so the cost grows linearly with how deep you page, becoming very slow on page 50,000. The alternative is keyset pagination: remember the sort key of the last row shown and fetch WHERE key > last_key ORDER BY key LIMIT n, which uses the index to jump straight to the next page in constant time regardless of depth. The trade-off is that keyset pagination does not support arbitrary jump-to-page-N, but for infinite scroll and next-page navigation it is dramatically better.

followUps.question: How do you delete millions of rows without locking the table?
followUps.answer: I delete in batches inside a loop: each iteration deletes a bounded number of rows (for example DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT 10000)) in its own transaction, then commits and briefly pauses. This keeps each transaction short so locks release quickly and the transaction log stays small, avoiding the table-wide blocking and log explosion of one giant DELETE. For deleting by a time boundary on a partitioned table, dropping or detaching the old partition is even better, since it is a near-instant metadata operation.

followUps.question: What strategies reduce read cost on a huge table beyond indexing?
followUps.answer: Partition pruning to skip whole partitions, covering indexes to avoid table lookups, and precomputed materialized views or summary tables for expensive aggregates so reads hit small derived data instead of the full table. Compression can reduce I/O, and moving cold historical partitions to cheaper storage keeps the hot working set small. Finally, pushing filters down and selecting only needed columns ensures the engine reads the minimum bytes. The unifying idea is to make each query touch the smallest possible slice of the table.

question: What is sharding, and how does it change the way you write SQL?
directAnswer: Sharding splits one logical dataset across multiple independent databases (shards), each holding a subset of the rows chosen by a shard key. It lets you scale writes and storage beyond a single machine. The catch is that SQL changes: queries that include the shard key go to one shard and stay fast, but queries that do not have to fan out to every shard and merge results, which is slow and limited. Cross-shard joins, global uniqueness, and transactions across shards become hard, so you design the schema and queries around the shard key to keep most operations single-shard.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Sharding is horizontal partitioning across separate database servers. Each shard is a full database holding a slice of the data, partitioned by a shard key such as customer_id or a hash of it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A single database server has limits on writes, storage, and connections. When vertical scaling and read replicas are not enough, sharding spreads the load across many servers so the system can grow nearly horizontally.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A routing layer maps each row and query to a shard using the shard key. A query that filters by the shard key is routed to exactly one shard and behaves like a normal single-database query. A query without the shard key (a cross-shard or scatter-gather query) must run on all shards and have its results merged, which is far more expensive and cannot easily do joins or ordering across shards. Because of this, you choose a shard key that matches your dominant access pattern, denormalize to keep related data on the same shard, and avoid operations that require global coordination.

whyImportant: Sharding is how large systems scale writes, and writing sharding-aware SQL is essential to keep them fast. Understanding the constraints (single-shard fast, cross-shard slow) shows you can design at scale, which is a strong senior signal in system-design and data interviews.
realWorldExample: A multi-tenant SaaS sharded by tenant_id so each tenant's data lived entirely on one shard. Almost every query already filtered by tenant, so it routed to a single shard and stayed fast. The rare cross-tenant analytics ran as a separate scatter-gather job, keeping the hot path single-shard.

nestedTopics.title: Choosing a shard key
nestedTopics.explanation: The shard key should appear in the vast majority of queries and distribute data evenly to avoid hotspots. A natural tenant or user id often works because most access is scoped to it. A poor key (like a low-cardinality status, or a time field that funnels all new writes to one shard) causes skew and hot shards.

nestedTopics.title: Scatter-gather queries
nestedTopics.explanation: Queries lacking the shard key must run on every shard and combine results, which is slower and cannot natively join or globally sort across shards. You minimize these by designing around the shard key, and when they are unavoidable you push aggregation down per shard and merge a small result, or run them as offline analytics.

nestedTopics.title: Cross-shard transactions and uniqueness
nestedTopics.explanation: A transaction spanning shards needs distributed coordination (two-phase commit or a saga), which is slow and complex, so you keep transactions within a single shard. Likewise, globally unique ids cannot rely on per-shard auto-increment; you use UUIDs or a central id generator so keys are unique across all shards.

followUps.question: How do you keep most queries on a single shard?
followUps.answer: You pick a shard key that matches the dominant access pattern (often tenant_id or user_id) and you include it in every query that can have it, so routing sends each query to exactly one shard. You also denormalize and co-locate related data under the same shard key so common joins stay within one shard. The goal is that the hot path never fans out, and only rare analytical queries become cross-shard, which you then handle separately.

followUps.question: What problems does sharding introduce that a single database does not have?
followUps.answer: Cross-shard joins and aggregations become expensive scatter-gather operations or are pushed to a separate analytics system; transactions across shards require distributed coordination that is slow and failure-prone, so you avoid them; global uniqueness and foreign keys across shards are not enforced by the database, so the application must manage id generation and referential integrity; and rebalancing data when you add shards or when one becomes hot is operationally complex. These costs are why sharding is a last resort after replicas, caching, and vertical scaling.

followUps.question: How is sharding different from partitioning and read replicas?
followUps.answer: Partitioning splits a table within a single database to aid pruning and maintenance, but all the data still lives on one server, so it does not scale writes beyond that machine. Read replicas copy the whole database to additional servers to scale reads, but writes still go to one primary. Sharding splits the data across independent servers so each handles only its slice, which is the only one of the three that scales write throughput and total storage horizontally, at the cost of the cross-shard complexity the others avoid.

question: When should you use CTEs, subqueries, temp tables, or derived tables for complex queries?
directAnswer: They overlap in capability but differ in readability and performance. CTEs make multi-step logic readable and support recursion, but in some engines they are an optimization fence that blocks predicate pushdown. Inline subqueries and derived tables usually let the optimizer merge and optimize them as one query. Temp tables physically store an intermediate result, which helps when you reuse it many times or when materializing breaks a bad estimate, but they cost I/O and statistics maintenance. The choice is readability versus the optimizer's ability to fuse everything, judged from the actual plan.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: These are four ways to express intermediate results in a complex query: a CTE (WITH clause), a subquery (nested SELECT), a derived table (subquery in the FROM), and a temp table (a physical scratch table). Each structures multi-step logic differently.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Complex analytics need intermediate steps. Different constructs exist to balance human readability against how much freedom the optimizer has to combine steps into one efficient plan, and to allow physically materializing a result when that is beneficial.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Subqueries and derived tables are usually inlined: the optimizer treats them as part of the larger query and can push filters in, reorder joins, and pick one global plan. CTEs are often inlined too, but some engines materialize them (a fence), running them once into a temp result the outer query cannot optimize through. Temp tables are always materialized: you compute and store the intermediate result, then query it, which adds write cost and lets you index it and gather fresh statistics, sometimes producing a far better plan when a single fused query misestimates badly.

whyImportant: Choosing the right construct affects both whether teammates can read the query and whether it runs in seconds or minutes. Knowing the optimizer-fence behavior and when materialization helps is a nuanced, senior-level distinction that interviewers value.
realWorldExample: A five-step analytical query written as nested CTEs was slow because the engine materialized an early CTE and could not push a date filter into it, scanning the full table. Rewriting the heavy step as a derived table let the filter push down and the query ran far faster; a different step that was reused three times was materialized into a temp table on purpose to compute it once.

nestedTopics.title: CTE as optimization fence
nestedTopics.explanation: In engines that materialize CTEs (historically PostgreSQL before 12, or when marked MATERIALIZED), the CTE runs as written and the outer query's filters are not pushed into it, which can read far more data than necessary. When that happens, converting the CTE to a subquery or derived table restores predicate pushdown.

nestedTopics.title: When to materialize with a temp table
nestedTopics.explanation: Materializing into a temp table helps when an intermediate result is reused many times (so you compute it once), when it is small after heavy filtering, or when the optimizer's estimate for an inline version is badly wrong and a fresh, statistics-bearing temp table yields a better plan downstream. The cost is the extra write and the loss of cross-step optimization.

nestedTopics.title: Readability versus optimizer freedom
nestedTopics.explanation: CTEs read top-to-bottom like steps and are great for maintainability, while deeply nested subqueries can be hard to follow. But the most readable form is not always the fastest, because inlining gives the optimizer more freedom. The pragmatic approach is to write for readability first, then check the plan and refactor only the steps that actually misbehave.

followUps.question: How do you tell if a CTE is being materialized and hurting you?
followUps.answer: I look at the execution plan: if the CTE shows up as a separately materialized result (for example a CTE Scan in PostgreSQL reading a precomputed set) and I see a filter being applied after it that I expected to apply inside it, that is the fence biting. The tell-tale sign is far more rows scanned in the CTE than the final result needs. I confirm by rewriting it as a derived table and comparing plans; if the filter now pushes down and rows drop sharply, the CTE was the problem.

followUps.question: Are temp tables always slower because they write to disk?
followUps.answer: No. While they do incur write cost, that can pay off in several ways: the intermediate result is computed once instead of repeatedly, the temp table gets its own accurate statistics that fix a downstream misestimate, and you can index it for the subsequent joins. For a result reused multiple times or one where inlining produces a terrible plan, a temp table is often dramatically faster overall despite the write. It is a trade-off you validate by timing both forms, not a blanket rule.

followUps.question: Does the choice matter the same way across all databases?
followUps.answer: No, it is engine-dependent. Modern PostgreSQL inlines non-recursive CTEs by default (so they behave like subqueries unless marked MATERIALIZED), SQL Server generally inlines CTEs, and other engines differ. Temp table behavior, statistics, and tempdb-style overhead also vary. So the right construct depends on your specific database version, which is why I always confirm with the actual execution plan rather than assuming behavior carries over from another system.

question: How does read replication affect SQL correctness, and what is replication lag?
directAnswer: Read replicas are copies of the primary database that serve read queries to spread load. The catch is replication lag: replicas apply the primary's changes slightly after they happen, so a read replica can return data that is a few milliseconds to seconds behind. This causes read-your-writes problems, where a user updates something then immediately reads a replica and sees the old value. You handle it by routing reads that must be current to the primary, and only sending tolerant reads (reports, lists that can be slightly stale) to replicas.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Read replication maintains one or more secondary copies of a database that continuously apply changes from the primary. Replication lag is the delay between a change committing on the primary and that change appearing on a replica.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Read-heavy applications can overwhelm a single server. Replicas let you scale reads horizontally and provide failover copies, but because replication is not instantaneous, they introduce a consistency trade-off.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The primary streams its write-ahead log (or binary log) to replicas, which replay it to stay in sync. Asynchronous replication, the common default, lets the primary commit without waiting for replicas, so it is fast but the replica trails by the lag. Synchronous replication waits for a replica to confirm before committing, removing lag for that replica at the cost of higher write latency. Applications must decide per query whether eventual consistency from a replica is acceptable or whether the read must hit the primary.

whyImportant: Replication is one of the first scaling tools teams adopt, and lag-related bugs (a user not seeing their own change) are common and confusing. Knowing how to route reads correctly and reason about consistency shows you can scale reads without breaking correctness.
realWorldExample: After a user updated their profile, the app immediately read it back from a replica that had not yet applied the change, so the UI showed the old name and the user thought the save failed. Routing the immediate post-write read to the primary, while keeping the heavy profile-list pages on replicas, fixed the confusion without giving up the read scaling.

nestedTopics.title: Asynchronous vs synchronous replication
nestedTopics.explanation: Asynchronous replication commits on the primary without waiting for replicas, giving low write latency but allowing lag and a small window of data loss on failover. Synchronous replication waits for at least one replica to confirm, eliminating lag and data loss for that replica but adding latency to every write. Many systems use semi-synchronous setups to balance the two.

nestedTopics.title: Read-your-writes consistency
nestedTopics.explanation: This is the guarantee that after you write something, your own subsequent reads see it. With async replicas it is not automatic. You provide it by routing a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or by tracking the write position and only reading from a replica that has caught up to it.

nestedTopics.title: Routing reads by tolerance
nestedTopics.explanation: The practical pattern is to classify reads: critical, must-be-current reads (immediately after a write, balance checks) go to the primary, while latency-tolerant reads (search results, analytics, list pages) go to replicas. This maximizes read scaling while keeping correctness where it matters.

followUps.question: How do you guarantee a user sees their own write with replicas?
followUps.answer: The simplest approach is sticky routing: for a short window after a user writes, send that user's reads to the primary so they always see fresh data. A more precise approach is to capture the replication position (log sequence number) at write time and, on the next read, only use a replica that has applied up to that position, otherwise fall back to the primary. Both ensure read-your-writes consistency without forcing every read onto the primary, preserving most of the scaling benefit.

followUps.question: What causes replication lag to spike, and why does it matter?
followUps.answer: Lag spikes when the replica cannot apply changes as fast as the primary produces them: a burst of heavy writes, a long-running transaction or large batch on the primary, single-threaded apply on the replica, or the replica being busy serving expensive read queries. It matters because the staleness window grows, so more reads return outdated data and, on a failover, more recently committed data could be lost with async replication. Monitoring lag and shedding load or throttling big writes keeps it bounded.

followUps.question: Can you run analytics on a replica safely?
followUps.answer: Yes, and it is a common pattern, because offloading heavy analytical queries to a replica protects the primary from their I/O and CPU load. The caveats are that the data is slightly stale (usually fine for reporting), and that very long analytical queries on the replica can themselves increase apply lag or conflict with replication on some engines. For heavy or long-running analytics, a dedicated reporting replica, or an asynchronous copy into a separate analytical store, isolates that workload cleanly from both the primary and the transactional replicas.
